Reviewer recommends rejection: Reject. The Berlin 9.58 record, Gay's 9.71, the Beijing times, the birth details and the three-Games sprint double are confirmed. Five cited sources could not be opened because the fetch tool limit was reached: yahoo-1919, aljazeera-2011, itv-2017, aljazeera-2017 and startribune-2008. That leaves unverified the Nesta Carter/methylhexanamine/IOC details, the 62-hundredths margin and the 19.20 scoreboard error, the Daegu new-rule detail and Blake's 9.92, and the 12 August hamstring fall, Britain's gold and the '14 medals'. Two fixes are needed: (1) the Tokyo 2025 claim and the present-tense 'siguen ahí'/'sigue teniendo' lines rest on a preview dated 14 May 2025 and need a current World Athletics records page or the Tokyo results; (2) the final sentence needs its own citation. The Olympics.com profile says his first 100 m record came in 2007, while Britannica gives May 2008 (the correct year). The article follows Britannica, but under the style guide the disagreement between the two cited sources should be handled explicitly or the Olympics.com citation dropped from that point. Re-run the fact check once the five sources can be opened.

claims.claim: Usain Bolt was born on 21 August 1986 in Sherwood Content, Trelawny parish, Jamaica (body, FAQ, person.json facts birthDate/birthPlace).
claims.note: The Olympics.com profile gives 21 August 1986 and Sherwood Content. Britannica gives 21 August 1986 and Trelawny parish. The nationality fact (JM) is confirmed by the Olympics.com profile, which lists Jamaica.

claims.claim: In August 2009 at the Berlin Worlds Bolt ran 9.58 for 100 m (16 August 2009) and 19.19 for 200 m.
claims.note: World Athletics (16 Aug 2009) confirms 9.58 in Berlin. The 19.19 is not in wa-958. Britannica confirms the 200 m record came four days later, and the yahoo-1919 article could not be opened. 'Four days' and the 20 August date are consistent with that.

It only supports the situation in May 2025. Cite the current World Athletics records list, or the results of Tokyo 2025, or reword.

claims.claim: The summary and the closing line say Bolt still holds the 100 m and 200 m world records ('sigue teniendo', 'siguen ahí').
claims.note: This is a present-tense claim. The only source is the May 2025 snapshot, and the closing sentence has no tag of its own. Today is 2026-10-26, so a current World Athletics records page is needed.

claims.claim: He grew up playing cricket and football, and his school cricket coach pushed him to take athletics seriously.
claims.note: The Olympics.com biography says exactly this.

claims.claim: In 2002, aged 15, he won the 200 m at the World Junior Championships.
claims.note: Britannica says he was 15 and won 200 m gold at the 2002 world junior championships. Olympics.com says 'by the age of 16, in 2002' he was world junior champion. The article's age is the one Britannica gives, and the two sources differ slightly.

claims.claim: His first 100 m world record came in May 2008.
claims.note: Britannica says 9.72 in New York four weeks after 3 May 2008, which is about 31 May 2008. The cited Olympics.com page says 2007, which is wrong. The article is right, but the discrepancy between the two cited sources is not mentioned.

claims.claim: In Beijing he lowered the 100 m record to 9.69, then won the 200 m in 19.30, another world record.
claims.note: The 9.69 comes from World Athletics (the Beijing record). The 19.30 and the 200 m world record come from Britannica.

claims.claim: The Jamaican relay team, with Bolt, also won gold in Beijing with a world record.
claims.note: Britannica gives 37.10 as a world record, and says the gold was later stripped.

claims.claim: In January 2017 the IOC disqualified the team because Nesta Carter's sample from those Games tested positive for methylhexanamine, a banned stimulant.
claims.note: The web_fetch tool limit was hit before this URL could be opened. Britannica confirms only that a teammate's failed drug test led to the gold being stripped. The month (January 2017), Carter's name, the substance and the IOC as the body are unverified.

claims.claim: Bolt's official record is eight Olympic golds, not nine (also summary and FAQ answer 1).
claims.note: Olympics.com lists 8G. Britannica says the relay gold was stripped. The FAQ detail (IOC, 2017, Beijing 4x100, Carter) rests on the unreachable ITV source.

claims.claim: In Berlin Bolt took another 0.11 s off his own 100 m record; Tyson Gay was second in 9.71, a US national record.
claims.note: World Athletics says 0.11 s off 9.69, and Gay second in 9.71, a national record.

claims.claim: On 20 August he won the 200 m final in 19.19 by 62 hundredths; the scoreboard first showed 19.20 before it was corrected.
claims.note: The Yahoo article could not be opened because of the fetch tool limit. The 0.62 margin and the 19.20 scoreboard error are not in any source I could read. Bloomberg, found through web search, confirms 19.19 four days after the 100 m.

claims.claim: At Daegu 2011 he was disqualified from the 100 m final for a false start under a newly introduced rule that eliminated the athlete on the first offence; Yohan Blake won in 9.92.
claims.note: The Al Jazeera page could not be opened. Britannica confirms the false-start disqualification in 2011. The new-rule detail and Blake's 9.92 are unverified.

claims.claim: He defended the 100 m and 200 m titles at London 2012 and Rio 2016, becoming 100 m Olympic champion at three consecutive Games.
claims.note: Britannica: golds in the 100 m and 200 m in 2008, 2012 and 2016. Olympics.com says he won the 100 m at three consecutive Games.

claims.claim: He chose the London 2017 Worlds to say goodbye; on 12 August, as anchor of the 4x100, he injured a hamstring and fell on the track while Great Britain won gold.
claims.note: The Al Jazeera page could not be opened. Britannica confirms the 2017 retirement, the hamstring injury in the relay final and Jamaica finishing eighth. The 12 August date, the anchor leg, the fall and Britain winning are unverified.

claims.claim: He retired with 14 World Championship medals.
claims.note: The source could not be opened. Britannica does not give the total.

claims.claim: Retirement came after the 2017 World Championships (summary).
claims.note: Britannica says he retired after the 2017 world championships.

claims.note: The figures are confirmed. 'Holder today' depends on the May 2025 snapshot (see above).
